content.title: Will the Artemis II launch be visible from Washington, DC? | How to watch
content.text: Updated April 1, 2026 3:51pm EDT Artemis II launch expected Wednesday evening NASA's Artemis II mission is scheduled to launch on Wednesday, April 1 from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch is the first manned mission to the moon in more than 50 years. FOX 5's Jen Delgado has the details. WASHINGTON - The Artemis II mission is set to launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Wednesday. It will be the first crewed mission to the moon in more than 50 years. Here's everything you need to know about the historic launch. RELATED: Watch live: NASA Artemis II launch time, astronauts, mission updates What time is the Artemis II launch? Timeline: The launch window opens at 6:24 p.m. Wednesday, but will stay open for two hours, meaning Artemis II could launch any time between then and 8:24 p.m. If the weather doesn't cooperate though, the launch will be scrapped and rescheduled for a later date. Though as of 1 p.m., officials say there's an 80% chance they'll be cleared for liftoff during the launch window. Can you see the Artemis II launch from DC? Stargazers will be looking to the sky Wednesday night in hopes of seeing Wednesday's historic launch, but the odds of seeing the crew blast off into space go down the further north you get from Florida. Credit: NASA According to NASA, most of Florida and some cities in south Georgia have the best chance of seeing the Artemis II rocket. But what about further north, like D.C.? Previous launches from Cape Canaveral, like SpaceX's Atlas V launch in March, were seen as far north as New Jersey, according to some reports. But, with scattered showers in the forecast across much of the DMV Wednesday evening, even if the rocket was visible, the weather likely means you won't see anything. How to watch Artemis II launch What you can do: FOX 5 will be streaming Wednesday's launch on the FOX Local app, and online at fox5dc.com. You can tune in right now to watch live coverage from Florida. The Source: Information in this story is from NASA, Delaware Online and previous FOX 5 reports. Air and SpaceNews
